chunks: Muhammad ibn Ali Majiluyah (may God be pleased with him) narrated that Muhammad ibn Yahya al-Attar quoted Muhammad ibn Ahmad, on the authority of Sahl ibn Zyad, on the authority of Al-Hussein ibn Sa'id al-Ahvazi, on the authority of Ibn Abi Umayr, on the authority of Hammad, on the authority of Al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)
He said: The people are divided into six groups: the weak, those who are reconciled, the expectant, those who confess to their sin and are hostile, and the believer.

key_terms.مَرْجُوٌّ: The expectant (those who hope for salvation or truth)
key_terms.مُؤَلَّفٌ: The reconciled (those whose hearts are won over by grace or authority)
key_terms.مُسْتَضْعَفٌ: The weak (those weak in faith or acceptance)
key_terms.مُعْتَرِفٌ بِذَنْبِهِ: One who confesses to their sin
key_terms.وَنَاصِبٌ: And the hostile (one who opposes the Imams/Truth)

ai.seo_question: What are the six groups of people according to Imam al-Sadiq in al-Khisal?
ai.summary: In this foundational hadith from *Al-Khisal*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) delineates the six spiritual states of humanity, a taxonomy that Shia scholars often interpret through the lens of *al-Jabr wa al-Tafwid* (determinism vs. free will) and political allegiance. This classification not only describes individual theological positions but also reflects the socio-political realities of the early Islamic community, distinguishing between those who are passive, those who are reconciled to authority, and those who are actively hostile or faithful. The 'hostile' (Nasib) group specifically refers to those who reject the Ahl al-Bayt, while the 'expectant' (Murji) often denotes those who delay judgment on the Imams, highlighting the critical role of *Wilayah* in defining true belief.
